title: Run, Serve, Change in Schools
author: Nick Hart
summary: Continuing his series on levels of work, Nick Hart translates Jaques's abstract framework into the more usable run / serve / change language and tests it against school life. Run work keeps the school functioning and is urgent, visible and noisy; serve work is the quiet structural layer that decides what is fixed, where decisions stop, and how contradictions are reconciled; change work shapes the future system over long time spans with weak feedback. He warns against mapping these onto hierarchy (teachers run, middle leaders serve, senior leaders change), insisting they are types of work that exist at every level. Using parent communication as a worked domain, he shows how mapping the full workload first reveals whether the issue is prioritisation, protection or genuine capacity, and how failures typically come from run work overwhelming everything, serve work becoming invisible, and change work arriving only episodically. He ends by arguing that what schools call these categories matters, proposing run, enable, design as the school-appropriate vocabulary.
points: Serve work is defined as structural rather than supportive: deciding what is fixed versus variable, where decisions stop and start, and what the default response is, so staff are not relying on personal resilience or goodwill.
Middle leaders end up carrying run work twice (teaching and leadership) with serve work squeezed into the margins, which Hart calls a structural load problem rather than a people problem.
Run, serve and change are types of work, not tiers of the hierarchy, echoing Jaques's point that everyone does immediate work and only the ceiling of judgement differs.
In parent communication, most failures are serve failures: no shared response-time expectations, no scripts for predictable situations, no escalation routes and no protected planning time.
Hart proposes renaming the categories for schools as run, enable, design, arguing that the words leaders use carry meaning and should be chosen deliberately rather than inherited.
quotes: Strategic work is defined by the level of judgement required and the time span over which decisions carry real consequences. Leadership pressures in schools are not necessarily caused by lack of effort or skill, but by different kinds of work being collapsed into the same roles, meetings and people.

Run work is essential but urgent, visible and noisy. It creates constant demand for attention and pulls decision making toward the immediate. Under pressure, this is where much school leadership time goes.

In schools, serve work often sits with middle leaders but without being clearly named or protected. When pressure rises, it is the first to be displaced by run work. Middle leaders then carry run work twice: teaching run work and leadership run work, with serve work squeezed into the margins or handled through goodwill and personal effort.
That reading mirrors school hierarchies but it fundamentally misunderstands the idea. Run / serve / change are not roles, they are types of work.

Each response is reasonable in isolation but when run work expands unchecked, leaders become trapped in short cycle responsiveness. Communication becomes reactive rather than intentional. The school feels busy but not coherent.
Serve work often exists informally, carried by conscientious individuals rather than embedded in systems. When it is not named or protected, it becomes invisible.
What we call things matters because words repurposed still carry meaning elsewhere. How we talk about anything in school should be decided deliberately, not inherited uncritically.
